newsitem.title: UK: Dlr firm in late Europe but capped at 1.73 marks.
newsitem.headline: Dlr firm in late Europe but capped at 1.73 marks.

text.p: The dollar moved lethargically in late European trade, unable to gain further after the surprise and dollar/mark buying sparked by a Bundesbank council member's comment on German interest rates faded away.
Dollar/mark had gained on Reimut Jochimsen's comment, made overnight, that he would not rule out another cut in German interest rates although he also said he did not see one.

Traders said mark/yen had been the big mover during European trade, saying its drop below a key technical support level of 65.90 yen had shored up dollar/mark and dampened dollar/yen after the impact of Jochimsen's comments wore off.
Mark/yen had been unable to crawl off its session low of 65.76 since early afternoon, which compares with 66.04/07 in late European trade on Wednesday.

"The dollar's done well against the mark today but not so well against the yen in Europe, and it was basically due to big (mark/yen) cross plays as opposed to any strong moves in the dollar," said one trader at a U.S. bank in London.

The dollar was just off its session high against the mark at 1530 GMT, quoted at 1.7275/79 against 1.7252/62 late on Wednesday. Against the yen, it was at the day's low of 113.40/45 against yesterday's 113.98/08.
Excitement over Jochimsen's words ebbed as the market realised his remark about not ruling out a rate cut did not seem to be signalling real action by the Bundesbank, analysts said.

"What else could he say? Since German interest rates are already at such a low level, (if he had not said that) it would really have pushed the market into taking a one-way view on rates, and that is something the Bundesbank has been very concerned about," said Klaus Baader, currency economist at Lehman Brothers.
As expected, the Bundesbank left its key interest rates unchanged when it held its regular council meeting today.

"It would be an extraordinary time for a rate cut. Inflation is not a problem in Germany, but for several months people have been underestimating it," Baader said. "Also, the mark is at three-year lows (against the dollar) day after day. It's a pretty compelling argument not ease policy further now."

Apart from the major dollar/mark and dollar/yen pairs the dollar's fortunes were mixed today, with the most noticeable move being its slide against the Canadian dollar after the Bank of Canada raised its key bank rate by 25 basis points to 3.50 percent.
The Canadian dollar shot up to the day's high of $1.3770 per U.S. dollar in the wake of the rate hike, compared with $1.3945/50 in late European Wednesday.

Meanwhile, the dollar was firm against the French franc on a comment by Bank of France policy committee member Jean-Pierre Gerard, who said a rate of 5.75-5.90 francs to the dollar was "a good balance" but that 6.20 would be more favourable for France.
Traders said the remark had boosted the dollar to a high of 5.8373 francs today compared with Wednesday's close of 5.8222/44, although it had eased back to yesterday's levels by late trade.

Apart from the dollar, the British pound continued to fare well against the mark today, hitting a new 59-month high of 2.8825. It had backed off to 2.8753/58 marks by 1620 GMT, although this was still well above late yesterday's 2.8685/95.
Expectations of higher interest rates in Britain have been bolstering sterling, with the pound reaching new 59-month highs against the mark nearly every day so far this week.
